name: Hair transplant laxometer

lead: A laxometer measures scalp laxity, meaning how much the skin of the back of the scalp can be pinched and stretched. In strip (FUT) hair transplantation, a strip of scalp is removed from the donor area and the wound is closed, so how loose the scalp is affects how large a strip can be taken.

The payoff for appearance is a better-planned donor area: a narrower, more closely closed wound can mean a finer scar that is easier to cover with hair. The device was introduced by hair surgeon Parsa Mohebi; the research base for the scalp version is small and mostly from its inventor.

paras: Surgeons use a clinical version at consultations to assess scalp laxity before surgery, and an intra-operative version just before the strip is cut. Patients who do scalp exercises to loosen the scalp are sometimes tracked with it. The reading helps decide the safe strip width.

The device itself is a non-invasive measuring tool. The surgery it supports leaves a linear donor scar and has a recovery period of around two weeks. Readings can be affected by subcutaneous fat and skin thickness and stiffness, and early devices were described as not always accurate.

angle.text: The laxometer is used by surgeons to plan strip hair transplants. A well-matched strip width can leave a finer donor scar, which is easier to cover with the remaining hair.

lead: A laxometer is a measuring device for scalp laxity, or skin mobility, used in hair restoration surgery [1]. In strip harvesting (follicular unit transplantation), a strip of scalp about 1 to 1.5 by 15 to 30 cm is removed from the donor area at the back of the head and the grafts are dissected from it; the scar left behind is thin and linear [2].

Surgeons use laxometer readings to judge whether the donor wound can be closed after the strip is taken, which helps reduce the chance of taking too much skin; the benefit is described as greatest for patients with high hair demand and limited donor supply [1]. The design is credited to Parsa Mohebi, who presented it to the International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery [1].

Laxometers also exist in other fields. A shoulder laxometer measuring inferior humeral head translation showed good to excellent reliability in a 2008 study, and an eyelid laxometer was proposed in a 2018 study [3][4]. For the scalp device, no independent peer-reviewed trials are listed in the reference literature [1].

paras: The laxometer measures how far scalp skin stretches vertically when pinched. It is used in pre-operative assessment for strip harvesting and, in an intra-operative version, immediately before the strip is removed [1].
Two types are described: a non-invasive clinical laxometer used at visits, including to track laxity after scalp exercises, and an intra-operative laxometer used during surgery [1].

Strip harvesting is the most common way of obtaining follicles for transplants, and leaves a thin linear scar in the donor area that hair usually covers; newer closure methods are said to give finer scars [2]. Laxity matters because the wound edges have to be brought together. Readings aim to show how wide a strip can be removed while still allowing closure [1].
Subcutaneous fat, skin thickness and stiffness affect readings, and earlier devices were described as not always accurate; a 2011 design aimed to improve precision [1].
The scalp laxometer was presented by Dr. Parsa Mohebi at an International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery annual meeting in Las Vegas; the year is not established in encyclopedic sources [1].

No studies found for the scalp laxometer in the peer-reviewed literature reviewed here. Related laxometer studies exist in other areas: a reliability study of a shoulder laxometer measured a mean inferior translation of 1.5 mm in healthy shoulders with intraclass correlation coefficients of about 0.74 to 0.76 [3], and a study of lax eyelid syndrome proposed an eyelid 'laxometer' alongside three earlier grading methods [4].

timeline.event: A scalp laxometer design is proposed to address accuracy concerns [1].
